claims.claim: Democracy is a form of government in which political power — influence over institutions, leaders, and policies — rests in the hands of the people.

The word democracy literally means rule by the people, from the Greek dēmokratia, coined in the mid-5th century BCE from dēmos ('people') and kratos ('rule') to describe the political systems of Greek city-states, notably Athens.
In a direct democracy, people participate directly in making government decisions; the classic example is ancient Athens, where citizens debated and voted on proposed laws in the Assembly.
In a representative democracy, citizens do not govern directly; they elect representatives to make decisions and pass laws on behalf of all the people.
The government of the United States can best be described as a republic, or representative democracy.
Democratic elections combine one-person-one-vote with competition among candidates for office; free elections and a free press are linked to government accountability.
Participation is a core feature of democracy: participation in government matters, and government cannot function without active participation by at least some citizens.
Representative democracies combine majority rule with protection of minority rights: people cannot be deprived of certain rights even if an overwhelming majority thinks they should be.
Democracies protect citizens' freedom of speech and the press.

The rule of law is the mechanism, process, institution, practice, or norm that supports the equality of all citizens before the law, secures a nonarbitrary form of government, and prevents the arbitrary use of power.

Civil society is the dense network of groups, communities, networks, and ties that stand between the individual and the modern state, and it is a familiar component of liberal and democratic theorizing.

Democracies vary and face challenges: civic engagement in the United States has been declining as small face-to-face groups give way to large impersonal organizations (Robert Putnam), and meaningful participation requires citizens who understand their interests and can evaluate political arguments.
The U.S. Constitution opens with the words 'We the People of the United States,' grounding the authority of the government in the people.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the United States is best called a democracy or a republic.
positions: Some writers reserve 'democracy' for direct rule by citizens and therefore call the United States a republic instead.
Others use 'democracy' broadly for any government in which political power rests with the people.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: OpenStax American Government 3e treats the terms as overlapping — the U.S. government 'can best be described as a republic, or representative democracy.' The lesson adopts that framing and does not take a side in the terminological dispute.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How inclusive the classic example of direct democracy actually was.
positions: Ancient Athens is routinely cited as the textbook example of direct democracy.
Athenian participation was restricted: only adult male citizens could attend the Assembly, while women, enslaved people, and foreign residents could not.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents Athens as the standard example, as OpenStax does, and states the restriction factually so the example is not romanticized.

sourceRecords.title: Democracy (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sourceRecords.provider: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Tom Christiano and Sameer Bajaj)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports the scholarly working definition of democracy as a method of collective decision making characterized by a kind of equality among the participants at an essential stage of the decision-making process; elections as formal equality of one-person-one-vote with competition among candidates; the accountability link between free elections, a free press, and government responsiveness (citing Amartya Sen); and the point that Athenian democracy combined direct democracy for lawmaking with sortition for choosing officials. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
